Did the 2026 Condo Loan Changes Make Your Building Harder to Finance?

By Paul Hankins, Founder, CEO and Broker, NMLS #281393BrickWood Mortgage, Surfside Beach, SC

The short answer

For some buildings, yes. Since August 3, 2026, Fannie Mae no longer allows its quick check of established condo buildings with more than 10 units. Each building now needs a full check of its budget, reserves, repairs and rental setup, or FHA approval. The same change dropped the cap on investor-owned units, which helps buildings with many rentals.

  • Full ReviewThe standard check for an attached unit in a building of more than 10 units
  • $10,000 a unitUnfunded repairs above this, due within 12 months, make a building ineligible
  • 10%, then 15%The share of the HOA budget for reserves, rising for applications from January 4, 2027
  • Small buildingsTwo to four units, and most five- to ten-unit buildings, skip the building review

What changed for condo loans in 2026

Fannie Mae removed the Limited Review option for condo buildings. Limited Review let a lender approve many established buildings with a shorter check. Lenders can no longer use it for loan applications dated on or after August 3, 2026. Freddie Mac, the other company that buys conventional loans, has its own condo rules, and we check the building against both.

Today a loan sold to Fannie Mae on a unit in an established building with more than 10 units goes through one of three paths:

PathWhat it means for you
Full ReviewYour lender reviews the building itself: the HOA budget, reserves, unpaid dues, repairs, insurance, lawsuits and how the building is used.
FHA project approvalIf HUD itself has approved the building for FHA loans, a conventional lender can rely on that approval.
A review by Fannie Mae itselfFannie Mae reviews the building directly. This is used for new buildings and special cases.

For established buildings under Full Review, Fannie Mae also dropped its 50% limit on units owned by investors. A finished building with many rentals is no longer turned down for that reason alone. A new or newly converted building still needs at least half its units sold to buyers who will live there or use them as second homes.

Smaller buildings are simpler. Fannie Mae waives the building review, apart from a few basic requirements, for detached condos, buildings of two to four units, and five- to ten-unit buildings that are not part of a larger development or master association.

Does this apply to my loan?

Yes, whether you will live in the condo, use it as a second home or rent it out. The building review depends on the building, not on how you use your unit. How you use the unit changes the loan itself: the down payment, and whether the rent can help you qualify. Our guide to second home vs investment property loans explains that part.

Your unit will beBuilding reviewWhat else changes
Your homeThe same reviewThe smallest down payment
A second home you rent some weeksThe same reviewA larger down payment; the rent cannot be used to qualify
A rentalThe same review, and the 2026 change removed the investor cap in established buildingsThe largest down payment

What makes a condo building fail the review

A building fails when Fannie Mae sees risk in the building itself. These are the reasons a building fails, from Fannie Mae's rules.

Repairs the building has not paid for

A building that needs critical repairs is ineligible until the work is done. Critical repairs include problems that could cause a major system to fail within a year, mold or water getting into the building, advanced deterioration, and a failed mandatory structural inspection. Unfunded repairs costing more than $10,000 per unit that should be done within 12 months also count. Repairs owners make inside their own units, and work already paid for by a special assessment, do not. Among the items Fannie Mae lists to consider are sea walls, elevators, waterproofing, stairwells, balconies, foundations, electrical systems and parking structures.

Routine upkeep paid from the normal budget does not count. Damage limited to one or a few units, which does not affect the whole building, does not count either.

A special assessment for a critical repair

A special assessment is an extra charge the HOA bills owners for a big project. Your lender reviews each one: what it pays for, when it was approved and whether the work has started, its total, how much is still owed and when it will be paid off. If the assessment is for a critical repair and the problem is not fixed yet, the building is ineligible.

Thin reserves or owners behind on dues

Under Full Review, the HOA budget must put at least 10% of its assessment income toward replacement reserves, the savings for roofs, elevators and other big items. For loan applications dated on or after January 4, 2027, that minimum rises to 15%. A professional reserve study can be used instead if it shows the building is adequately funded. No more than 15% of the units may be 60 or more days behind on their HOA dues.

Ownership and commercial space

RuleLimit
Units one person or company may own, building of 21 or more units20% of the units
Units one person or company may own, building of 11 to 20 units2 units
Commercial space, such as shops, restaurants or a hotel section35% of the building

An evacuation order

A building under a full or partial evacuation order for an unsafe condition is ineligible until the condition is fixed and the building is declared safe.

Condotels and buildings with a rental desk

Fannie Mae will not buy a loan on a unit in a building that is run like a hotel, even when each unit has its own owner. A building can be treated as a hotel when it has any of these:

  • an HOA licensed as a hotel, motel, resort or hospitality business;
  • a rule that owners must put their unit in a rental pool, or share rental profits with the HOA or a rental company;
  • hotel services such as registration services, daily cleaning or central key systems;
  • "hotel", "motel" or "resort" in its name, unless that is only history;
  • marketing as a hotel, motel, resort or investment opportunity.

Owning a unit you rent out yourself is not the problem. The building's setup is. Our second home guide explains how a rental program changes your own loan. A building where owners rent on their own, with no required pool and no front desk, can still pass.

How FHA treats condos

An FHA loan on a condo needs the building to be FHA-approved, or the single unit to get a Single-Unit Approval, which still has to meet HUD's building standards. A building meant for rental for transient or hotel purposes cannot get FHA approval. If you plan to use an FHA loan, we check the building's approval status first. See our FHA loans page for the loan itself.

What to do if the building does not qualify

A building that fails Fannie Mae's rules is called non-warrantable. You can still finance it. BrickWood is a mortgage broker, so we can take the loan to lenders who keep loans in their own portfolio or offer programs outside Fannie Mae's rules. These loans usually ask for a larger down payment and cost more than a conventional loan. We show you the terms side by side before you decide.

A lender can also ask Fannie Mae for an exception when a building misses one rule but is otherwise sound. That takes time, so it works best when we start before you sign a contract.

Two related options:

  • If you will rent the unit, a DSCR loan qualifies you on the rent instead of your income.
  • If you are self-employed, a bank statement loan uses your deposits instead of tax returns.

Our affiliate Chapter3 Realty (see the disclosure below) explains how buyers approach these buildings in non-warrantable condos in Myrtle Beach and condotel financing.

What we check before you make an offer

  1. The building's name and status. We check the building's status with the lender and on HUD's list of FHA-approved condos.
  2. The HOA's papers. We request the condo questionnaire, budget, reserve study and insurance from the HOA or its manager.
  3. Repairs and assessments. We ask about inspections, planned work and every special assessment.
  4. The rental setup. We check for a rental pool, a front desk or hotel services.
  5. The right loan. You get a plain list of the loans the building looks likely to fit, and what could stop each one.

Doing this before the offer means your contract's financing deadline is not spent waiting on a building review. We lend on condos across the Grand Strand, from Myrtle Beach to North Myrtle Beach.

Condo loan questions

What is a non-warrantable condo?

A non-warrantable condo is a unit in a building that does not meet Fannie Mae's building rules, so a conventional loan on it cannot be sold to Fannie Mae. Common reasons are hotel-style operations, unfunded critical repairs, one owner holding too many units, or too much commercial space. You can still finance it with a portfolio or non-QM loan.

Did Fannie Mae get rid of Limited Review for condos?

Yes. Fannie Mae's Lender Letter LL-2026-03 retired Limited Review for all loan applications dated on or after August 3, 2026. Units in established buildings of more than 10 units now need a Full Review, FHA project approval, or a review by Fannie Mae itself.

Can I get a conventional loan on a condo I plan to rent out?

Yes, if the building passes the review. Renting your own unit is allowed. The building fails if it requires a rental pool, requires owners to share rental profits, or offers hotel services such as registration services or daily cleaning.

Does a special assessment stop a condo loan?

Not always. Your lender reviews each special assessment. If it pays for a critical repair that is not yet fixed, the building is ineligible. A special assessment for routine work does not stop the loan by itself.

How much must a condo HOA keep in reserves?

Under Fannie Mae's Full Review, at least 10% of the HOA's assessment income must go to replacement reserves, rising to 15% for loan applications dated on or after January 4, 2027. A professional reserve study showing adequate funding can be used instead.

Do small condo buildings need a review?

Often not. Detached condos, buildings of two to four units, and five- to ten-unit buildings outside a larger development or master association skip the full building review. A few basic requirements still apply.
